CASE REPORT
A 55-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital for
the ﬁrst time in 2005 because of a suicide attempt. She was
already diagnosed as having depression 4 years earlier. Her
symptoms began in 2001, after a gynecologic operation
(hysterectomy and oophorectomy because of leiomyoma). At

that time she was depressed, complaining of abdominal pain and
attempted suicide for the ﬁrst time, with medications. Two
consequent operations did not reveal an organic cause for the
pain and so the patient started psychiatric treatment. Her
mental status partially improved with paroxetine and she was
able to work again with occasional sick leaves.
In the meantime she was hospitalized in another
psychiatric department where computed tomography of the
brain was performed, showing moderate cortical cerebral
atrophy. Her level of functioning remained poor and so she
was retired.
At the time of admission to our hospital, in 2005, her
personal medical history included hypercholesterolemia, hyper-
tension, and the previously mentioned operations. Her family
history was negative for psychiatric and autoimmune disorders.
Her father died at a young adult age, after the operation of a
brain tumor. The patient did not use alcohol or other
psychoactive substances but she smoked a few cigarettes a day.
The patient presented with a subjective sensation of
tremulousness (what she called an ‘‘inner tremor’’), fatigue,
avolition, initial insomnia, early morning awakening, loss of
interest, and low mood. There were no signs of psychosis. We
noticed aﬀective incongruence between her subjective feeling of

a depressed mood and nondepressive facial expressions. She was
well oriented and knew some recent political events. Ideas of
hopelessness and guilt were present. Because she persistently
complained of an ‘‘inner tremor,’’ a neurologic examination was
performed but no parkinsonian signs were found. The clinical
impression was that depression and incipient psychoorganic
syndrome, detected by psychologic examination, were the main
reason for the patient’s disability.
When the patient was hospitalized again in January 2007,
the neurologic signs became apparent: cerebellar ataxia
with inability to stand or walk alone, stiﬀ gait, tension of
paravertebral musculature with hyperlordosis, resting tremor of
the left arm (greater amplitude that is typical for parkinsonian
tremor), discrete resting tremor of the right arm, and diﬀusely
low muscle tonus and muscle strength. Her facial expression was
reduced and speech was normal but monotonous. Deep tendon
reﬂexes were present, with normal plantar response. Deﬁcits in
sensibility were not found.
The subjective sensation of tremulousness was still
present. She seemed anxious and depressed and felt relatively
good only while lying on bed, staring at 1 point. Transitory
horizontal nystagmus and dilated pupils were occasionally
observed and tachycardia (up to 130/min) with tachypnea was
present. She was conscious and well oriented to time, place, and
persons, during the whole time. Her answers to typical questions
were correct, although given after a period of latency. However,
intellectual decline was obvious.
Routine laboratory ﬁndings were normal and repeatedly
checked. Creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase enzymes
were normal. Thyroid hormones, thyrotropin, corticotropin,
and cortisol were also within the reference range. Gastroscopy
revealed erosive gastritis. Gynecologic examination, transab-
dominal ultrasound, and standard chest and abdominal x-rays
did not show abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging of the
brain showed somewhat larger third and lateral ventricles with
larger frontotemporal bilateral subarachnoid spaces. Analysis
of cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) showed: a clear and colorless
appearance of CSF, normal total cell count, normal total
protein, glucose, and chloride levels; Pandy reaction was weak
opalescent. CSF protein electrophoresis showed: increased
prealbumin (7.8%; reference range: 4 to 7) and g globulin
(19.5%; reference range: 7 to 12), whereas albumin, a 1 globulin,
a 2 globulin, b 1 globulin, and b 2 globulin were within the
reference range. g globulins were divided into fractions.
Examination of the blood-brain barrier showed the presence
of oligoclonal immunoglobulin G bands suggestive of intrathe-
cal synthesis of g globulins. A test for serum autoantibodies to
GAD was positive (680 IU/mL; normally <10 IU/mL; cut-oﬀ
value for very high elevation: >250 IU/mL). Serologic tests for
borreliosis and neurotrophic viruses were performed. Only tests
for herpes simplex virus 1-IgM and IgG were positive.

The patient’s syndrome started insidiously with
aﬀective changes and abdominal pain, perhaps the
underlying abdominal pain was a trigger for the onset
of SPS. In general, the anxiety and depression observed in
our patient may be the result of, or a reaction to, the
underlying neurologic disorder or the 2 conditions may
exist comorbidly. Because psychiatric symptoms occurred
before the onset of obvious motor symptoms, the authors
believe that anxious depression, cognitive decline, and
neurologic signs seen in the patient are the primary
manifestations of the disease itself, forming a unique
syndrome. Our hypothesis is consistent with previous
observations that depression or other psychopathologic
symptoms may precede SPS symptoms.
15 The therapeutic

resistance of depression to diﬀerent antidepressants also
supports this hypothesis. Even tricyclic antidepressants,
known to worsen the course of SPS, 24 applied according
to treatment guidelines for depression, before the onset of
the physical symptoms of SPS were ineﬀective. Anxious
and depressive symptoms in SPS could be explained by
alterations in GABAergic neurotransmission.
